lines.text: Remember, almost every colossal squid ever studied had been caught dead or dying, on a fishing line or inside a whale.
On the ninth of March, 2025, a research ship called Falkor too was working near the South Sandwich Islands in the South Atlantic.
The team was driving a robot submarine called SuBastian, and its camera was live streaming to the internet.
About six hundred meters down, something floated into the lights.
It was a squid, only about thirty centimeters long, and it looked almost see through.
One of the scientists said it looked like a glass sculpture.
At first nobody on the ship was sure what it was.
Two squid experts, Kat Bolstad and Aaron Evans, went through the footage, and they confirmed it by the hooks on its arms.
It was a colossal squid. A young one. The first time one had ever been filmed alive in its natural home.
And that happened almost exactly a hundred years after the species got its name from two arm crowns in a whale.
It was not a monster. It was a teenager, only about as long as a ruler.
Its skin cells let it switch between see through and colored, so a young one can almost vanish.
An adult can grow to about seven meters long, and around five hundred kilos.
And nobody has filmed a live adult.
We know it by its eyes, its hooks, and what whales leave behind. We know very little about how it lives.
For a hundred years, this animal was a story told by whale stomachs and fishing lines. Now, for the first time, we had seen one living.
So what would you ask a colossal squid, if you could meet one? Tell me in the comments.
